items.text: SEASON 8 · EPISODE 3 · DRAFT · CASE-042  Studio theatre · Maya, Kit, Bram and Odile · Level L5 · Advanced support (formulas on request)  The studio theatre ceiling closed two weeks early. The loudspeaker supports are still on a pallet — and one hatch opens onto nothing.  ⚑ RV-160: sequence is the general contractor’s. RV-162: nobody in the story works at height; lifts belong to the trade using them. Some choices run on a clock.

items.title: The Ceiling Went Up First
items.stakes: A finished ceiling, sixteen missing loudspeaker supports — and a hatch that opens onto nothing.
items.clock: Before the ceiling contractor leaves site on Friday.
items.reward: Supports in, a room with no holes, and a ceiling that never closes early again.

objectives.text: Decide how the ceiling gets reopened
Open the ceiling without making it worse

items.rumor: Everything behind a ceiling is somebody's.

items.alt: The studio theatre with seats going in and a finished, closed acoustic ceiling overhead; Kit points up at it; Maya looks up.

bubbles.text: Closed. All of it. Our supports are still on the pallet.

items.caption: Two weeks ahead of the schedule everyone else was using.

lines.text: Closed. All of it. Our supports are still on the pallet.
Then nobody cuts anything until Bram sequences it. Get me the hatch schedule.

items.text: Act I — “The ceiling went up first”

items.prompt: 10:15. The AV contractor wants to cut in from below “where the loudspeakers go”. What do you do?
items.risk: A ceiling cut up by the wrong trade — or a theatre without loudspeakers.
timeout: The AV crew starts marking circles on the tiles.
The ceiling contractor sees them and stops work in protest.

hints.text: Who owns the order of trades — and what does he need from you?

options.label: Let them cut in
options.result: Bram: “Nobody cuts my ceiling contractor's work.”
options.consequence: Directing one trade into another's work.
options.fail: Sequence and trades are the GC's.

options.label: Ask Bram to stop any further closure; give him exact loudspeaker positions and the hatch schedule so he can sequence the ceiling contractor to reopen
options.result: Bram holds the last two bays and asks for positions by tonight.
options.consequence: Stop it growing, through its owner, with the information he needs.

options.label: Surface-mount loudspeakers below the ceiling instead
options.consequence: Changes the design to hide a sequence error.

options.label: Leave it until after opening
options.result: A theatre with no loudspeakers in its ceiling.

items.title: The ceiling went up first.
items.body: The GC's lookahead moved the studio ceiling from week 21 to week 19 to recover float. The change note went to the ceiling contractor — not to AV, electrical, mechanical or fire, all of whom had work above it. The gap between two trades was a line on a schedule nobody else saw.
items.label: Test: whose gap is it — and what should have come first?

items.sub: Advanced · the skill behind this chapter

items.alt: A teaching moment: Maya_Site and Kit_Site beside a board. Five-metre ceiling, ears at one point two, ninety-degree loudspeakers. RFI fifty-eight took out S-9. What does that do? Coverage across is two times three point eight — seven point six, so each cone reaches three point eight. Without S-9, the seats under it are five metres from the nearest loudspeaker. A hole right where the critics sit. S-9 goes back — and the hatch schedule gets fixed with it.

items.text: 📙 ON REQUEST · ADVANCED  Terms   Access hatch   Backbox   Ceiling loudspeaker   Construction sequence   If you need it   ƒ Ask for the formula · Ceiling loudspeaker spacing   ƒ FORMULA · Ceiling loudspeaker spacing  D = 2 × (H c  − H e ) × tan(θ ÷ 2)   D  spacing for edge-to-edge coverage at ear height, m  H c   ceiling height, m  H e   ear height — about 1.2 m seated  θ  the loudspeaker's coverage angle, degrees      ƒ Ask for the formula · Percentage   ƒ FORMULA · Percentage  % = part ÷ whole × 100   part  the piece you are measuring  whole  everything it is part of

items.label: **Sequence it:** open a finished ceiling without making it worse.

items.title: The hatch over nothing.
items.body: Kit checks positions against the RFI log. RFI 58, answered in March as value engineering, deleted S-9 and moved S-8 a metre east. Nobody updated the hatch schedule: one hatch was cut over empty space, and S-8 has no hatch at all. And without S-9, the seats beneath it — rows F to H — are 5.0 m from the nearest loudspeaker, whose coverage at ear height reaches 3.8.
items.label: Test: are those seats covered — and what did the RFI leave behind?

items.alt: A reflected ceiling plan: sixteen loudspeaker positions on a 5.0 m grid with their coverage circles; S-9 crossed out in red with a hole in coverage; notes: RFI 58 deleted S-9, seats 5.0 m from a loudspeaker.
items.caption: A hole where the critics sit.

items.prompt: Wednesday evening. What happens to S-9?
items.risk: A permanent hole in the studio theatre's coverage.
timeout: The RFI waits for next week's meeting.
The ceiling closes again without S-9.

hints.text: When will fixing S-9 ever be cheaper?

options.label: Leave it out — don't add work while the ceiling's open
options.result: Rows F–H hear the show 6 dB down and muddy.
options.consequence: Keeps the hole to save a support.
options.fail: A coverage hole is a design failure.

options.label: Restore S-9 by RFI response through Odile while the ceiling is open — the cheapest moment it will ever have — and re-issue the hatch schedule so S-8 gets its hatch
options.result: Odile issues it that night; Dario agrees the small cost; the hatch schedule is re-issued.
options.consequence: Fix the design while it's cheapest; fix the documents with it.

options.label: Turn S-5, S-10 and S-13 up 6 dB
options.result: The seats under them get loud; the hole stays a hole.

options.label: Ask Dario to decide, without numbers
options.result: Dario: “What does it cost, and what does it fix?”
options.consequence: An owner can't decide on adjectives.

items.title: The acoustic tile
items.body: In 1914 the acoustician Wallace Sabine and the vault builder Rafael Guastavino Jr. patented a sound-absorbing ceramic tile, used to tame echoing stone churches and halls. It was one of the first ‘acoustic’ ceilings — and it raised the question every ceiling since has had to answer: what has to go in behind it before it closes?

items.text: ✦ UX RULE #74 · AVERY'S LENS  Close nothing until everything behind it is signed  A finished surface hides everything behind it. Make closing it a checkpoint every trade behind it signs.  The studio theatre ceiling closed two weeks early. Sixteen loudspeaker supports were still on a pallet — and one hatch opened onto nothing.

items.alt: The reflected ceiling plan after the fix: all sixteen positions with overlapping coverage circles, S-9 restored; notes: hatches re-issued, survey rows F–H within 3 dB.
items.caption: Sixteen loudspeakers, sixteen hatches.

items.prompt: I closed it to save two weeks. You want me to lose them again?

options.label: “Four days, not two weeks — if we do it once, in order, while your ceiling crew is still here. And we fix S-9 while it's open.”
options.reply: Four days. Once. Positions on my desk by tonight.

options.label: “Who else is above that ceiling?”
options.reply: …Fire, electrical, mechanical. Let me call them.

items.title: delete S-9 (VE)
items.body: RFI 58, March, answered by the previous design lead: ‘Delete S-9, move S-8 1.0 m east — saves 2,400 (illustrative).’ No coverage check attached. The hatch schedule, sheet A-522, wasn't touched.

items.prompt: Friday. When may a ceiling close from now on?
timeout: The rehearsal room ceilings close early.

hints.text: What check would have stopped this on Monday of week 19?

options.label: Ask the ceiling contractor to wait for AV next time
options.result: Next time it's the sprinkler fitter who's behind.

options.label: Ceiling closure becomes a hold point on the GC's schedule: no area closes until AV, electrical, mechanical and fire sign above it and the hatch schedule is checked against the latest RFIs
options.result: Bram adds it to the lookahead template that afternoon.
options.consequence: Hidden work signed before it's hidden.

options.label: AV installs first everywhere
options.result: The sprinkler mains go in after your loudspeakers — through them.

options.label: Nothing — it was a one-off
options.result: The rehearsal rooms close early the week after.

items.text: FIELD NOTE —  Sequence belongs to the general contractor; closing a ceiling should be a hold point every trade above it signs. Hatch schedules follow the equipment through every RFI. When value engineering deletes a loudspeaker, check coverage: D = 2 × (H c  − H e ) × tan(θ ÷ 2), and spacing ≤ D ÷ √2 on a square grid. Fix the design while the ceiling is open — it will never be cheaper.
REFLECTION (optional)  · What gets “closed” at your work — a release, a report, a room — before everyone behind it has signed?
